memory_candidates.content: To prove a guarded build wrapper script (lake-build-guard.sh or similar) actually dispatches to its underlying tool rather than merely parsing arguments, use a fake-binary test seam: point the wrapper's *_BIN env var (e.g. LAKE_BUILD_GUARD_LAKE_BIN) at an executable stub in a scratch dir containing a minimal project marker file (e.g. a bare lakefile.toml), have the stub echo its argv and exit 0, then run both a negative control (the old/broken invocation, asserting the expected failure AND that the stub was never reached) and a positive proof (the corrected invocation, asserting the stub's echoed argv appears on stdout). Pass any 'never replay a cached result' flag the wrapper offers (e.g. --no-share) on the positive-proof run so a cached prior result can't produce a false pass. This is stronger evidence than a parse-only check.

When auditing a source store for a broken invocation pattern via grep, a single literal grep pattern (e.g. the exact tool-invocation string) can miss a compressed prose restatement of the same defect (e.g. a table-like summary line such as "Full project: `--` (no module)" that never spells out the full command). Run a second grep pattern targeting the prose-summary vocabulary (e.g. "Full project", "no module", "unscoped") to catch sites the literal-invocation grep misses.
